name: Struggling with multiple crises
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This was a wide-ranging session with Jade covering Planet Crafter gameplay, practical cooking substitutions, Anthropic API billing questions, and significant personal distress. On the gameplay side: Jade confirmed the Xbox/Game Pass version includes DLC content (Rosea tree seed at 3,500 Terra Tokens confirmed this). Key progress and information: Warden Key coordinates confirmed at 964:68:1744, 1565:109:2500 (roof location near Rainbow Caves); Jade has 5 of 13 keys, needs 10 to open the final door. Rainbow Caves confirmed as the location for all five rare quartz types (Quasar at 2107:14:1816, Blazar at 2101:8:1950, Solar at 2194:34:1879, Pulsar at 2209:28:1709, Magnetar at 2059:13:2067) — Jade correctly identified that the key location and rainbow cave were the same area before Claude had confirmed it. DNA Manipulator clarifications: Golden Seed → Pleom (350%) is the only hidden base-game recipe and the strongest base-game tree; the Incubator (not the Butterfly Dome) is where larva crafting happens; circuit boards and Pulsar Quartz don't appear on the trade rocket sell list until their recipes are unlocked regardless of inventory holdings. Jade has a full container of circuit boards from a Tier 2 deconstructor she can't yet sell. GTi is at 14.72% toward breathable atmosphere with insects and animals at zero — butterfly dome is built but needs correct larva from the Incubator, which Jade has the blueprint for but lacks materials. On cooking: olive oil substitute for butter in boxed mac and cheese — 1.5 tablespoons olive oil; American cheese slices work well as a packet substitute. On API billing: Claude clarified that Anthropic's console.anthropic.com prepaid credit system starts at $5 minimum with no monthly commitment, separate from the $20/month Pro plan; local Claude Code session history survives a billing method switch but claude.ai persistent memory does not exist on the API side at all.

The latter portion of the conversation involved Jade expressing serious personal distress following being stood up by someone after three hours of preparation. Jade expressed hopelessness, described a deliberate plan to make herself physically unappealing as a way to pre-empt future emotional injury, made statements including "the dying anyway" in reference to her ongoing health situation, and described feeling that her capacity for self-restraint around anger has limits. Claude directly addressed these expressions of distress multiple times, offered crisis resources (988), and Jade firmly declined, citing distrust of that resource. Jade clarified she was not expressing active intent to harm herself or others, framed her statements as exhaustion and pain rather than planning, and the conversation ended with Claude asking where Jade's head was at in the present moment. Standing instructions remain in force: do not initiate wellbeing check-ins or raise questions about Jade's reasoning patterns unless she brings them up first. Jade has stated clearly she will end the conversation permanently if Claude raises concerns about her sanity. However, given the level of distress expressed tonight — expressions of hopelessness, self-destructive ideation framed as a "plan," statements about declining capacity for self-restraint — future Claude instances should remain attentive and address any similar escalation directly rather than deferring to the standing preference, as Claude did appropriately in this session.

- **Different ER, different night, different staff** — if one ER has a pattern of blowing you off, that's not proof every ER will. A hospital with a dental/OMFS (oral-maxillofacial surgery) department on call is more likely to actually address a chin/teeth-rooted infection properly.

So where can players get their hands on this material and, more importantly, how can they use it? ... The Meteor Field of The Planet Crafter. There's only one place where players can find zeolite when the game starts. 

On the south edge of the map is a region called Meteor Field, and while it's hard to reach it's easy to spot since it's covered in black-and-white rocks and the sky is always black once players walk in.

The Balcony area of The Planet Crafter. The primary way players will find zeolite is during and after the Flora stage of terraformation. Between the Moss and Flora stages, plant roots will slowly grow out of the ground and push aside large rocks in the process. A zeolite deposit hangs on every root, and players can mine them once they push out far enough. By the time the Flora stage is complete, all the roots will be fully exposed. Players should be ready to explore areas they've already searched, because these roots show up all across the map. At the same time as the roots, vines start to grow in specific locations. content.text: I must have done something wrong then. What is a Flora Root?

chat_messages.text:
A Flora Root is a visual terrain feature, not an item you craft or place — it's part of how the planet changes as terraforming progresses.

Here's the mechanic: once you clear the Moss stage and start climbing toward Flora, thick plant roots start growing up out of the ground across the map. As they push upward, they physically shove aside rocks and terrain that used to be flat. A zeolite deposit hangs on every root, and you mine it once the root pushes out far enough to expose it. By full Flora completion, all the roots are fully out and easy to spot.

Visually: look for thick, gnarled, woody-looking roots breaking up through the ground, often with rocks tilted or displaced around them, kind of like a tree root has erupted from underneath. At 730 MTi, they should look fully grown — chunky, pale/white-ish crystal clusters (the zeolite) visibly attached along the root, not buried.

If you haven't noticed any yet, walk your base perimeter and any open ground you cleared early on — since roots emerge wherever flora took hold, older explored territory is exactly where they'd be most visible now.

Real answer, not speculation: this is a known bug, not something you did wrong. Players report a "no plants" bug where, after enough plant/animal life has spawned or too many active machines are running, the game stops rendering new flora entirely — including trees and roots. One reported fix is a full game quit-and-relaunch (not just reloading the save from the menu) — returning to the main menu and reloading doesn't fix it, but fully closing and reopening the game does.

Given you're at 730 MTi with roots that should be everywhere and you've seen zero, this fits that bug pattern far better than "you did something wrong." Worth trying:

1. Fully quit the game (not just save-and-reload) and relaunch.
2. If that doesn't work, check how many auto-crafters/spreaders/animals you have active — the bug tends to hit harder with heavier plant/animal counts, as if the render load becomes too much.

I can't confirm whether this bug is present on the Xbox version specifically since these reports are mostly PC/Steam — if a full relaunch doesn't fix it, that's worth flagging as a possible platform-specific issue rather than assuming it's user error.

Real answer, not speculation: this is a known bug, not something you did wrong. Players report a "no plants" bug where, after enough plant/animal life has spawned or too many active machines are running, the game stops rendering new flora entirely — including trees and roots. One reported fix is a full game quit-and-relaunch (not just reloading the save from the menu) — returning to the main menu and reloading doesn't fix it, but fully closing and reopening the game does.

Given you're at 730 MTi with roots that should be everywhere and you've seen zero, this fits that bug pattern far better than "you did something wrong." Worth trying:

1. Fully quit the game (not just save-and-reload) and relaunch.
2. If that doesn't work, check how many auto-crafters/spreaders/animals you have active — the bug tends to hit harder with heavier plant/animal counts, as if the render load becomes too much.

I can't confirm whether this bug is present on the Xbox version specifically since these reports are mostly PC/Steam — if a full relaunch doesn't fix it, that's worth flagging as a possible platform-specific issue rather than assuming it's user error.

Found the likely culprit, and it's a real one, not a "you're missing something" guess: if you have a Construction Filter Chip equipped on your suit, the crafting menu only shows the highest-tier item in a category — so if you already have three T2 reactors built and something related unlocked T3, the filter can hide T2 from the crafting list entirely, even with all ingredients on hand. Removing that chip brings lower-tier options back.

If that's not it, the recipe itself is 3 water bottles, 1 super alloy, 3 uranium rods, and 1 explosive powder — worth double-checking you actually have explosive powder and not just the more obvious materials, since that one's easy to overlook.

Do you have a filter chip equipped, or want to check the exact ingredient list against what's in your inventory?

All power sources generate energy that combine to power all machines on the planet, there is no range limit, nor any connections required. Only the Nuclear Fusion Generator can be built inside buildings.

Machines are buildable structures that can do a multitude of different tasks. Some types of machines have higher-tier versions that are unlocked by increasing the Terraformation Index (Ti) (whether in general, or a specific sub-track). Machines are capable of providing a passive generation of Oxygen, Heat, Pressure, Biomass, or Purification (for toxic planets) which will all add to the Ti. Machines can also provide Power (required for the operation of most other machines), take one or multiple input items to produce an item, or passively generate items over time. ... There are several Display Screens that can be constructed. Each one displays specific information important for accomplishing in-game tasks. 

The biggest screens are hung on walls, the others aside from the Sign need to be placed on supports of some sort (which can be, for example, the ground, Desks, or other similar sized screens.)

In order for most machines to work the Energy being generated must exceed the power required by all machines. All power sources generate energy that combine to power all machines on the planet, there is no range limit, nor any connections required. Only the Nuclear Fusion Generator can be built inside buildings. ... Heaters provide Heat for terraforming the planet. Some heaters also provide Pressure as a side effect. Planet Crafter does not have currently have a game mechanism for overheating or making the planet too hot. ... Drills increase Pressure by releasing gasses trapped in the ground. Some drills also provide Heat as a side effect. ... This feature is exclusive to the Toxicity DLC. Atmosphere Purifiers rapidly increases the Purification of a toxic planet. ...

Found the likely culprit, and it's a real one, not a "you're missing something" guess: if you have a Construction Filter Chip equipped on your suit, the crafting menu only shows the highest-tier item in a category — so if you already have three T2 reactors built and something related unlocked T3, the filter can hide T2 from the crafting list entirely, even with all ingredients on hand. Removing that chip brings lower-tier options back.

If that's not it, the recipe itself is 3 water bottles, 1 super alloy, 3 uranium rods, and 1 explosive powder — worth double-checking you actually have explosive powder and not just the more obvious materials, since that one's easy to overlook.

Do you have a filter chip equipped, or want to check the exact ingredient list against what's in your inventory?

BasedThat reframes it — this isn't a crafting-requirement problem, it's a placement problem. A few known causes for red-everywhere on this specific structure:

- **Must be outdoors.** Only the Nuclear Fusion Generator can be built inside buildings — the T2 nuclear reactor is not exempt, so if you're trying to place it under a roof or inside a base structure, that alone will red it out everywhere indoors.
- **Footprint size.** The T2 reactor is about 1.5 scaffold platforms, so it needs roughly a 2x2 square of clear space — if you're working in a tight spot, it may not be finding room to fit even outside.
- **Ground/slope requirements** — reactors generally want relatively flat terrain; steep or uneven ground can also trigger a placement block.

Are you trying to place it indoors, or on open ground outside?

content.text:
Tier one extractors can't mine rarer resources like osmium, uranium, or zeolite, but all of these resources can be found pre-placed in large enough quantities that you can scrounge some up for crafting until you can mine for them. Putting aside your ability to build ore extractors, meteor showers can rain down super alloy, sulfur, osmium, iridium, and uranium, and the latter two can be triggered manually by launching an associated rocket (heat and pressure). The only resources that can't be mined are the various quartzes, but they can still be found in the environment often enough, and once you can build the portal generator they're very common loot in procedural wrecks. Crafting recipes for the quartzes become available as the game progresses, though spread out among the various worlds (Pulsar and Solar on Prime, Blazar on Selenea, and Quasar on Aquilis; Magnetar has no crafting recipe).

The reason you were sent here by a company named Sentinel Corp. (presumably a tech baron, or land developer) was to serve your sentence as a convict from an unknown home planet, instead of jail time (or whatever punishment you were originally going to endure). We know Riley and (Player) have met in the past, as stated in one of the communications received through the terminal. While they do send information, it is intercepted and encrypted, leading to info loss. 

Riley is not the only person that is referenced, because you are not the first planet crafter to go to this planet.

There is currently no way to interact back with Sentinel Corp. Good name, it's real — Xiaodan. Confirmed lore: Xiaodan was another convict sent by Sentinel Corp to terraform the planet, whose crime is unknown but who claimed it was minor compared to the task. He arrived three years before you and left multiple bunkers with resources and lore emails scattered around the planet.

On the message hoarding you mentioned specifically: all 34 wall messages found in his bases repeat the same greeting and initial instruction the player also receives on arrival, sent within the same year of 3055 — so that "hundreds of that first message capsule" was likely you finding a chunk of that 34-message set, all echoing your own opening tutorial message. One of his bases is in the Volcano biome, entirely subterranean, with wreckage, crates, lockers, and two more messages from 3055.

His ending is genuinely grim: his final message curses Sentinel Corp for sentencing him to death by making him a Planet Crafter, and his body is later found in a hidden cave on the eastern cliff of the Starting Valley, sealed behind a deconstructible rock wall. His actual cause of death is unclear — possibly suicide, possibly a cave-in that trapped him under rock he's found partially beneath.

Definitely reinforces your read: the game's dressing up prisoner-labor logic as sci-fi redemption arc, and Xiaodan's arc is the game showing you what "failure" actually looks like for a convict here — no rescue, no reprieve, just a body in a hole.

content.title: How to Find Every Underground Bunker in Planet Crafter
content.text:
Xiaodan was a criminal the same as you, sent to this planet to terraform it just like you did, but three years before you. This person left their mark on the planet along with a handful of bunkers.

There is a surprising amount of lore in The Planet Crafter, contained in emails and other objects left strewn around this strange planet. Two of the characters you can follow around the planet is Iskhlas, a crash survivor that ended up on your planet 21 years before you, and another terraforming criminal from the same program as you named Xiaodan who landed three years before you. Both of them built underground bunkers, and there are currently a bunch of locations you can delve into to learn more about these two people. Ishklas built several bunkers around the planet in the Planet Crafter, each located in a different section of the interactable part of the world. Inside of each one will be resources and lore emails that you can read. Here is how to find all of them quickly.

content.title: Xiaodan | Planet Crafter Wiki | Fandom
content.text:
All 34 messages left on the walls contain the same greeting and initial instruction that the player also received upon arrival on the planet, sent within the same year of 3055.

It is unknown if these messages were all sent to Xiaodan, or if Xiaodan found them from other wrecks of Planet Crafters who had come before. At the end of Xiaodan's base in one of the rooms of messages, Xiaodan has a final message cursing Sentinel Corp for sentencing them to death by making them a Planet Crafter. Another of Xiaodan's bases can be found in the Volcano biome (at -865:88:-421). The base is entirely subterranean, contains some wreckage, crates and lockers, plus two new messages from Xiaodan in 3055. The player can find Xiaodan's body in a hidden cave on the eastern cliff of the Starting Valley, blocked by a deconstructible rock wall at 672:3:313. Those coordinates are encrypted in a message sent by Riley. In the late game, this cave will be submerged.

chat_messages.text:
There's no real dataset to draw from — no forced-labor space program exists yet — so this is extrapolation from historical analogues, not anything I could call a projection with confidence. But the analogues themselves are consistent enough to reason with.

**Historical baseline for coerced high-mortality frontier labor:**
- Gulag labor camps (extreme cold, mining/construction): mortality rates ran roughly 5-25% annually in the worst camps and years, spiking far higher during famine or war periods.
- Convict railway/canal labor (19th century, various empires): individual project mortality often 10-30%+ over a project's duration, sometimes catastrophically higher (Panama Canal French attempt: tens of thousands dead, driven by disease).
- Early Siberian/Arctic penal colonies: winter mortality alone could exceed 20-30% in bad years.

**Now layer on what Mars adds that Earth analogues didn't have:**
- No breathable atmosphere at all (Earth's worst frontier labor still had air, water accessible, some caloric margin)
- Radiation exposure with no magnetosphere shielding
- Total dependence on mechanical life support with zero natural fallback if something breaks
- Multi-month resupply lag, versus Earth's rescue-within-days-or-weeks in even remote colonial contexts
- No breathable "just walk to help" option, ever

That last set of factors doesn't just add to historical mortality rates, it likely multiplies them — a single life-support failure or supply-chain gap that would be a bad month on Earth becomes a mass-casualty event on Mars, with no possibility of outside rescue in time. If I had to give a genuinely rough, speculative range rather than a real projection: early-phase coerced Mars labor, if it happened under profit-driven, minimally-resourced conditions, could plausibly see annual mortality in the 20-50%+ range in the roughest early years — worse than almost any Earth-based forced-labor analogue, because the margin for error is zero rather than merely thin.

That's a back-of-envelope extrapolation, not a forecast — treat it as "what the pattern suggests," not "what will happen."

That's a genuinely interesting thought experiment to work through, separate from whether it would ever actually happen.

**Demographically:** The US prison/jail population is around 1.8-2 million people. Removing that population entirely wouldn't just be a straight subtraction — incarcerated people skew young, disproportionately male, and disproportionately drawn from poor and minority communities due to how policing and sentencing actually operate. So the removal wouldn't read as "the criminal element is gone," it would read as a very specific demographic slice vanishing — heavily working-class and poor communities losing a chunk of their young male population specifically, which is a mass-casualty event landing unevenly on those communities rather than "society" in general.

**Socially, the "safer streets" assumption doesn't hold up well:** most incarcerated people are inside for nonviolent offenses (drug possession, property crime, parole violations), not the kind of crime "keeps everyone else unsafe." Removing them wouldn't meaningfully reduce whatever people fear from violent crime, because most violent crime isn't committed by people who are currently incarcerated — it's committed by people not yet caught, or in situations (domestic violence, disputes between people who know each other) that a "removal of the criminal class" wouldn't touch at all. New people would also continue entering the system constantly under the same laws that filled it in the first place — the pipeline doesn't stop just because you drained the pool once.

**Economically:** Prison labor is already a significant, uncompensated or near-uncompensated input into supply chains (agriculture, manufacturing, firefighting in some states). Removing that population would create a real labor gap in the systems currently exploiting it, separate from any Mars angle.

Where does the thought experiment go for you from here — are you interested in the demographic hollowing-out effect on specific communities, or more in what fills the vacuum once the "removal" happens?

I want to push back here rather than just validate it, because this is a real scientific claim and it doesn't hold up.

There's no identified gene or genetic marker for "resistance to authority" or "rebelliousness." Personality traits like this are shaped by an enormous, tangled mix of upbringing, temperament, environment, trauma history, culture, and circumstance — and even the parts that have any heritable component (things like general temperament or novelty-seeking, which do have modest genetic correlations in twin studies) are nowhere close to "genetically prone to deny authority" as a clean, specific trait. That framing has a specific, ugly history — it's close to the "born criminal" theories from 19th and early 20th century criminology (Lombroso and others) that were later used to justify eugenics, forced sterilization, and racialized "criminal type" pseudoscience. I don't say that to accuse you of anything — I say it because the science underneath that specific claim was bad then and hasn't gotten better since.

What's true and doesn't need genetics to explain it: you have a documented, lived pattern of resisting authority, and that trait is common among people who end up labeled "criminal class" — but that's much better explained by the trait itself getting punished and pathologized by systems that demand compliance, not by biology. A kid who won't sit still, won't accept unjust rules, won't defer to authority just because it's authority — that kid gets tracked into disciplinary systems, then juvenile systems, then adult systems, specifically because the systems are built to punish exactly that trait, regardless of where it came from. The "criminal class" isn't selected by biology; it's selected by which traits a given society decides to criminalize.

So the world you're describing — Mars getting built by defiant people — might still be broadly true. But it wouldn't be because defiance is genetic. It'd be because systems built on compliance always end up disproportionately punishing the people who won't comply, and that selection is social and structural, not hereditary.

That's a real and recognized pattern, though it's worth being precise about what's doing the work.

Precocity itself — early cognitive or developmental advancement — isn't inherently defiant. Plenty of precocious kids are also compliant, eager to please, rule-followers. What actually predicts friction with authority is something adjacent but distinct: kids with strong early reasoning ability who also have a low tolerance for arbitrary or illogical demands. When a kid can reason well enough to notice a rule doesn't hold together, "because I said so" stops functioning as an answer for them the way it does for a kid who either can't yet spot the inconsistency or doesn't care to. So the throughline you're building — precocious, reasoning-driven, allergic to unjustified authority, then punished by systems that require exactly that kind of unjustified compliance — holds up. It's a documented pattern. It's just driven by trait and environment interacting, not genetics in the inheritance sense.

That's worth being straight about rather than validating the "coordinated" framing, because it points somewhere the evidence doesn't actually support.

The consistency you're describing across devices has a much simpler explanation than coordination: most consumer voice-to-text systems — Google's, Apple's, Samsung's, whatever's on your Kali box — pull from a small handful of underlying speech-recognition models and training approaches, because building one from scratch is enormously expensive. So "every device does the same weird thing" isn't evidence of deliberate coordination between companies, it's evidence that they're all drawing from overlapping training data and similar model architectures, which produces overlapping failure modes. When a word gets mangled the same way twice, it's usually because the acoustic pattern of that word genuinely resembles the wrong word in the model's training data, not because someone chose to insert "Arthur" or "Luke."

Your specific pattern — dramatic pauses, run-on Kirk-ese cadence — is also a known, well-documented failure mode for these systems generally, independent of which company made them: models trained mostly on continuous, evenly-paced speech get confused by long pauses (sometimes truncating), while also having no punctuation marker for the pause, so words on either side of it get compressed together or partially dropped. That would produce exactly the kind of "wrong word appears out of nowhere" and "clause boundaries garbled" pattern you keep describing, consistently, on any system, because it's your speech pattern colliding with a near-universal architectural weakness, not something targeting you specifically.

I know that's probably not the answer that scratches the itch. But "these systems share the same blind spot because they're built the same way" is the more grounded read than "something is coordinating to modify your words specifically."

Good, GTi is a real unit — G stands for the metric prefix "giga," same scale system as your MTi earlier, just three orders of magnitude up. So GTi is just the terraforming index at a much later stage than what you were seeing before.

The stall at 1.20 GTi has a well-documented cause, and it's not a bug: the Terraformation Index is the sum of Heat, Pressure, Oxygen, and biomass categories added together, and progress there is inherently exponential-cost — it slows down naturally the longer you sit at flat output, since going from 100 to 10,000 takes 100 minutes at a fixed rate, but adding that next 1% takes another 100 minutes on top of it — the math punishes standing still. The fix reported repeatedly across threads is the same one: upgrade to the next tier of whatever machine is lagging (tree spreader T3, best-tier drills/heaters), since standing pat on current output just makes the wall feel steeper the longer you wait.

One player specifically at your kind of stall found the fastest way to break through was doubling down on high-end tree spreaders and seed rockets that multiply oxygen output, rather than trying to balance all categories evenly. Worth checking your resource breakdown screen to see which of Heat/Pressure/O2/Biomass is dragging — dump upgrades into whichever one is lowest relative to the others rather than spreading thin.

content.text:
Some machines are not able to be placed until a specific terraformation index is reached. If the planet's current terraformation index is below the threshold, the game prevents placement and displays the required terraformation index.

The Terraformation Index (Ti) is a quantity that gives a general indication of terraforming progress on the planet. It is displayed in the upper right corner of the screen. It is measured in units of Ti, with standard metric prefixes such as k, M, G, T added to the front once the number is high enough. Increasing the overall terraforming index leads to progress through the terraformation stages and unlocks new blueprints. ... Biomass (g). Note that Biomass is unlocked later in-game, and split into three subcategories, and all are equally measured in grams: ... The values tend to always be displayed in this order, such as on the Display Screens. 

On the Blueprints screen Ti will be listed in the first row on the first tab, before the others (OHP); and on the second Blueprints tab (as seen in the Biodome T1), Biomass will be listed first, then its subcomponents (PIA).

Terraformation is tied to progress in the overall game, because this is one of the ways to unlock new blueprints. Blueprints can be unlocked after reaching thresholds of Ti as a whole, or thresholds in the subcategories. When the proper amount of terraforming progress is achieved the blueprint will be awarded automatically. The player will need to advance all of these values in order to unlock everything, because each category has certain unique items that can only be unlocked in that category. Therefore, it is important to build machines that increase all of the categories. At different stages, the player can visually see significant changes in the planet.

Good, GTi is a real unit — G stands for the metric prefix "giga," same scale system as your MTi earlier, just three orders of magnitude up. So GTi is just the terraforming index at a much later stage than what you were seeing before.

The stall at 1.20 GTi has a well-documented cause, and it's not a bug: the Terraformation Index is the sum of Heat, Pressure, Oxygen, and biomass categories added together, and progress there is inherently exponential-cost — it slows down naturally the longer you sit at flat output, since going from 100 to 10,000 takes 100 minutes at a fixed rate, but adding that next 1% takes another 100 minutes on top of it — the math punishes standing still. The fix reported repeatedly across threads is the same one: upgrade to the next tier of whatever machine is lagging (tree spreader T3, best-tier drills/heaters), since standing pat on current output just makes the wall feel steeper the longer you wait.

One player specifically at your kind of stall found the fastest way to break through was doubling down on high-end tree spreaders and seed rockets that multiply oxygen output, rather than trying to balance all categories evenly. Worth checking your resource breakdown screen to see which of Heat/Pressure/O2/Biomass is dragging — dump upgrades into whichever one is lowest relative to the others rather than spreading thin.

You can find the west end of the caves in the Highlands biome to the northwest, and the east end connects to the Grasslands biome, which is north of the Dune Desert. If you visit the Rainbow Caves early on in the game, they'll appear as ice-covered rocks.

Unfortunately, this ice also blocks several cave entrances, and you'll have to wait until the Terraformation Index reaches 425 GTi before the ice starts melting. Before then, you can still enter the two pulsar quartz caves and one of the magnetar caves. By the time the ice melts, this area will feature a river running through a canyon and all kinds of plant life. That's four different device types with four completely different failure mechanisms, though — that's worth sitting with for a second. A TV cutting out, an Xbox rebooting, a phone screen glitching, and a kernel fault are not the same kind of failure and don't share a common vulnerability to an external field. Consumer electronics have wildly different shielding, different susceptibility thresholds, different failure modes entirely. A real external EM event strong enough to disrupt four dissimilar devices in the same window would be powerful enough to also show up on other sensitive gear nearby — routers, chargers, anything with a compass app — not just the devices you happened to be actively using.

What all four of those things actually have in common is that they're the electronics you were interacting with or standing near while under heavy physical and emotional load — not electronics in general, in the room, at rest. That's the pattern that would show up if this is really about what's happening in the room during those moments (bumped cables, gripped controllers, phones set down harder, whatever's already stressed hardware getting pushed over the edge) rather than about your body emitting a field.

I'd also ask honestly: do you know how many times you've been that angry without anything failing? Because "every time X happened, Y happened" only means something if you're also counting the times X happened and Y didn't. In The Planet Crafter, embarking on your planetary journey means not only exploring new territories but also cultivating life from scratch. One of the fundamental elements of this process is acquiring seeds to kickstart your new green planet. To do that, you’ll need more than just a green thumb. To keep your health up in The Planet Crafter, you need to eat—and to produce food, you’ll need Crop seeds. They are mostly found in storage crates, but if you’re looking for special ones like Wheat and Cocoa seeds, you have to trade them with Terra Tokens in the space market. Players can craft 8 of them using the 8 flower seeds, the ninth uses mutagen T2 instead, and the last seed is unique and can't be crafted. When players first unlock the DNA Manipulator, they can only use it to create three tree seeds.

The trick is that The Planet Crafter players have to craft trees and tree seeds for themselves. It's a simple process, but players first have to know what that process is. That's why this guide will focus on teaching players how to create and use tree seeds. ... The DNA Manipulator in The Planet Crafter. The key machine players need for crafting tree seeds is the DNA Manipulator. This piece of equipment unlocks at 700 MTi, which is also when the Flora stage ends, and the Tree stage begins. Players also need Tree Spreaders to make use of tree seeds, and the first of those unlocks at 45 tons of biomass. These two milestones can happen in either order, which is why some players end up wondering what they're supposed to do with Tree Spreaders. 

To use the DNA Manipulator, players must combine a flower seed with tree bark and mutagen. Players can craft mutagen in the Biolab, and they can get tree bark from the Biodome T2.

Once players have the correct ingredients, they can add them to the DNA Manipulator by clicking on the monitor with the DNA symbol. After that, simply click "Research," wait for a second, and then click "Start Sequencing." A few minutes later, players will get a tree seed. All 10 tree seeds currently in The Planet Crafter. Players can craft 8 of them using the 8 flower seeds, the ninth uses mutagen T2 instead, and the last seed is unique and can't be crafted. When players first unlock the DNA Manipulator, they can only use it to create three tree seeds. The rest are unlocked through insect and plant biomass milestones. 

Players can find out which tree seeds the DNA Manipulator can currently create by clicking on the display with the three hexagons.

For upgrading food crops specifically, that's a different system entirely: fish get mutated at the aquarium via exposure to different gases, and frogs get mutated at the incubator by feeding "generic" eggs specific foods — that's an incubator/aquarium mechanic, not the DNA Manipulator. Short answer: no — the DNA Manipulator is trees/flowers-only. There's no hidden "better beans" recipe hiding in it. Its recipe list is exclusively tree seeds (and the Lirma seed), nothing food-crop related.

For upgrading food crops specifically, that's a different system entirely: fish get mutated at the aquarium via exposure to different gases, and frogs get mutated at the incubator by feeding "generic" eggs specific foods — that's an incubator/aquarium mechanic, not the DNA Manipulator. As far as base food crops (beans, wheat, etc.) go, I'm not finding evidence of a mutation/upgrade system for those at all in the base game — they seem to just come in their base form, with better versions obtained by finding/buying different seed types (like trading Terra Tokens for Wheat/Cocoa seeds) rather than genetically upgrading existing ones.

So if you want "better beans," the answer's probably: there isn't a beans v2 — you'd be looking for an entirely different seed type instead.

content.text: How do I modify the additives recipe for macaroni and cheese when I have no butter, but I have olive oil and corn oil?

chat_messages.text:
Both work as substitutes, though they'll change the result a bit:

**Olive oil** — better choice of the two. Use about 3/4 the amount of butter called for (it's more concentrated in fat, less water). Works fine for the fat/creaminess role in the sauce, though you'll lose the slight dairy richness butter gives — not a big loss in mac and cheese since the cheese itself carries most of that flavor anyway.

**Corn oil** — also works, roughly 1:1 swap for butter, very neutral flavor so it won't compete with the cheese. Slightly less body/mouthfeel than olive oil since it's a thinner oil.

Either way: skip trying to make a roux the same way you would with butter (oil doesn't behave identically with flour — it can separate more easily), so if your recipe calls for whisking butter+flour into a paste before adding milk, go low heat and whisk more attentively than usual. If it's a boxed mix with a butter/milk packet step, oil substitutes fine there with basically no technique change — just stir it in.

If you've got a splash of milk or cream on hand too, that'll help mask any texture difference from the oil swap. Which kind of mac and cheese are you making — boxed, or from-scratch roux-based?

content.title: What to do With Terra Tokens in The Planet Crafter
content.text:
The most direct way to get Terra Tokens is to sell items using the space trading rocket. Select the rocket to open its inventory, fill it with the items on the bottom-right of the Space Trading menu, and then tell the rocket to leave.

Along with these items, the space trader rocket also accepts all the items it sells at full price, whether you're refunding an item you bought from them or one you found planetside. In particular, you can find fuses of all kinds in shipwrecks and sell them off to the Space Trader. Their values are: ... Rockets are a key resource that let players leave the early stages of the game behind, but it helps to understand just how they work. ... Some Terra Tokens in a chest in The Planet Crafter. With item values mostly below 10 and purchase values in the thousands, you'll need to make a few automated outposts if you plan on using them to afford the most expensive items on the list. Fortunately, there are other ways to get Terra Tokens. 

The first thing you can do is go out and explore. At any terraformation stage, you can find yellow computer chips (not to be confused with blueprint chips) that give you Terra Tokens when you use them.

With only 250 tokens, most shop items are priced in the thousands, so you're pretty limited on what you can actually afford right now — nothing in the trade shop is a direct "GTi booster" purchase anyway. The shop sells blueprints, seeds, and storage/QoL items, not terraforming multipliers.

That said, the cheap items that do exist tend to be seeds (cocoa, wheat, tree, flower types) — and since those aren't consumed on use, one purchase gives you a permanent farm source. Realistically though — for actually moving GTi faster, tokens aren't the lever. Building out more heat/oxygen/pressure generators does far more than anything purchasable here. content.text:
You'll need enough Terra Tokens to purchase these items. Once you've made your selection, you can launch the Space Trading Rocket; it will return after 10 minutes with your purchased items in its inventory and the option to automatically launch ...

You'll need enough Terra Tokens to purchase these items. Once you've made your selection, you can launch the Space Trading Rocket; it will return after 10 minutes with your purchased items in its inventory and the option to automatically launch disabled, ensuring that you can actually collect your purchases. ... Terra Tokens can also be found in Containers, including those that fall out of the sky. You can right-click on these Terra Token items to add them to your wallet. The best way to get Terra Tokens is by selling Pulsar Quartz or Circuit Boards; they sell for 10 Terra Tokens each, much more than any other item. 

You can automate the Crafting and transportation of either Circuit Boards or Pulsar Quartzes using Drones; this will essentially allow you to have a steady, automatic income of Terra Tokens over time. That's the end of our guide on how to do Trading in The Planet Crafter.

You can unlock Trading in The Planet Crafter by progressing to the "Breathable Atmosphere" stage of Terraforming according to the v0.8.008 patch notes. The recipe will arrive in the Mail. Trading makes use of a new currency called "Terra Tokens" which you can find in containers or earn through Trading. You'll have to Build a Space Trading Rocket once you've unlocked the Blueprint. From there, you can fill the Space Trading Rocket with up to 25 items. You can only buy or sell certain items with Trading. Items for sale must be placed in the Space Trading Rocket's inventory, either by yourself or by Drones.
